analysis.one_liner: Requires large companies to audit and disclose child labor in their supply chains, with fines up to $100 million.
analysis.headline: Sponsored by a single senator with no cosponsors, the bill went no further than the Senate committee and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require U.S.-listed companies with more than $500 million in annual revenue to audit their entire supply chains — including suppliers and contractors like cleaning and food-service firms — for unlawful child labor. Each year they would file a report with the Labor Department, publish it publicly, and have their CEO certify its accuracy under penalty of perjury. The Labor Secretary could fine a company up to $100 million for a false report and up to $500 million for retaliating against workers who cooperate with an audit. The bill never received a committee vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers — especially minors and migrant youth — who end up in unlawful jobs through large companies' supply chains and contractors. The bill creates confidential, off-site audits with pay-stub checks and retaliation protection, and forces public disclosure so consumers, investors, and the Labor Department can see which companies found violations.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Child and migrant workers in supply chains

how_it_helps.text: Covered companies must run annual supply-chain audits that include confidential off-site interviews with a cross-section of workers, including any minors present, and a review of payroll, age-verification, and labor-broker records.

Companies must publish the audit report on their website and file it with the Labor Department, and the Secretary must report to Congress each year which companies failed to audit or were found to have used unlawful child labor.

The Labor Secretary can impose civil damages of up to $100 million on a company that violates the reporting requirement, up to $500 million on a company or contractor that willfully retaliates against audit participants, and can seek court injunctions where violations endanger workers.

The bill bars companies, suppliers, and contractors from retaliating against workers for talking to auditors and requires contracts to extend the same grievance protections to audit participation as to any other workplace complaint.

analysis.who_pays: Large publicly traded companies with over $500 million in annual revenue bear the cost of annual audits, compliance staffing, and possible penalties, and some of that cost may pass through to prices; suppliers and contractors found using unlawful child labor would lose a workforce they can legally no longer employ.
analysis.who_pays_short: Corporations with over $500 million in revenue

drawbacks.text: Every company above $500 million in revenue — roughly thousands of large firms — would have to conduct detailed annual audits covering an extensive list of records and worker interviews, a substantial recurring compliance cost even for companies with clean records.
CEOs must personally certify compliance or disclosure under the federal False Statements Act, exposing individual officers to legal jeopardy over supply chains they cannot fully observe.

The bill covers only companies with over $500 million in gross receipts, leaving smaller firms and their supply chains outside the reporting requirement, and its main remedy for a company that simply files an inaccurate report is a civil fine rather than direct relief for exploited child workers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The compliance burden is real but the bill's purpose — getting independent eyes on supply chains where child labor has been documented — addresses a harm that falls on children who cannot protect themselves. The chief design weakness is that it relies on disclosure and fines rather than direct enforcement against the employers of underage workers, and it exempts companies below the $500 million threshold.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which took no action on it, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Josh Hawley introduced the bill on May 3, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No other senator cosponsored the bill; the cosponsor list shows zero.
The committee took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — and no additional actions appear in the bill's history after the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporations and their suppliers and contractors are better off because the bill died: they avoid annual supply-chain audits, public disclosure of child-labor findings, and civil penalties that could reach $100 million or $500 million.

for.name: Sen. Josh Hawley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate HELP Committee.

against.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded committee action on the bill — no hearing, markup, or vote — during the two years it sat in the committee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only one sponsor, a Republican, and zero cosponsors from either party, so no meaningful partisan pattern formed; it never reached a vote.

industries.industry: Large public corporations (over $500 million in annual revenue)
industries.note: The bill would obligate these companies to audit and publicly disclose child labor across their supply chains and face civil penalties up to $100 million for false reports. Their interest in avoiding the audits and liability runs against the public's interest in knowing where child labor appears.

industries.industry: Labor brokers, staffing firms, and on-site service contractors (cleaning, food service, maintenance)
industries.note: Contractors and brokers who supply workers to large companies would be swept into the audits, and any that had placed underage workers would face disclosure and potential fines up to $500 million for retaliation. Firms profiting from cheap unlawful labor would lose that business.
The bill mandates annual supply-chain audits and explicitly asks companies to disclose whether verification was done by a third party, creating recurring demand for independent audit work.
